moments.title: Moorish invasion of Iberia
moments.body: An Umayyad army crosses the Strait of Gibraltar and rapidly conquers most of the Iberian peninsula.
moments.takeaway: Spain's medieval history is also Islamic history.

moments.title: Toledo retaken
moments.body: The fall of Toledo is a turning point in the Reconquista. Its translation schools transmit classical texts (via Arabic) to the rest of Europe.
moments.takeaway: War and scholarship moved in step.

moments.title: Granada falls
moments.body: The Nasrid Emirate surrenders. The 800-year Reconquista ends. The Alhambra Decree expels Jews months later.
moments.takeaway: 1492 is one of the most consequential single years in European history.

now.title: Al-Andalus today
now.body: Cordoba, Seville and Granada conserve major Islamic monuments. Sephardic citizenship has been offered to descendants of expelled Jews.
now.open_questions: How does Spain narrate its Muslim and Jewish past?

items.reflection: Modern Spain was forged across eight centuries of contact and conflict.

moments.title: Isabel and Fernando marry
moments.body: The marriage joins Castile and Aragon, beginning unified Spanish monarchy.
moments.takeaway: Modern Spain begins with a marriage contract.

moments.title: Columbus reaches the Bahamas
moments.body: Columbus's voyage opens transatlantic colonisation. His diary records Tainos as 'gentle and peaceful'.
moments.takeaway: Colonisation's earliest documents preserve indigenous voices to the extent the colonisers chose to record them.

moments.title: Treaty of Tordesillas
moments.body: A papal-mediated line divides the non-European world between two Iberian powers.
moments.takeaway: Empire was divided on paper before being claimed on land.

now.title: 1492 today
now.body: Hispanidad Day (12 October) is a Spanish national holiday, increasingly contested in the Americas as 'Indigenous Resistance Day'.
now.open_questions: How should October 12 be commemorated?

items.reflection: The Atlantic became Spanish before any other European country crossed it.

moments.title: Cortes lands in Mexico
moments.body: Cortes burns his ships and marches inland with around 500 men.
moments.takeaway: Strategic decisions can decide empires.

moments.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
moments.body: After siege and smallpox, the Aztec capital falls. It becomes Mexico City.
moments.takeaway: Indigenous allies and disease were essential to Spanish conquest.

moments.title: Inca emperor killed
moments.body: Pizarro captures Atahualpa and later executes him despite a ransom of gold. The Inca empire is conquered.
moments.takeaway: Within twelve years, two of history's largest empires fell.

now.title: Conquest's memory
now.body: Mexico's president Lopez Obrador formally requested an apology from Spain in 2019. Restitution of artefacts is ongoing.
now.open_questions: How should colonial histories be apologised for, if at all?

items.reflection: The Spanish empire in the Americas began in two violent decades.

moments.title: Cervantes at Lepanto
moments.body: Cervantes loses the use of his left hand at the Battle of Lepanto. He calls himself 'the one-handed of Lepanto'.
moments.takeaway: Literary biography is also military biography.

moments.title: Don Quijote part 1
moments.body: The novel's first part, parodying chivalric romance, becomes an instant bestseller in Spain and France.
moments.takeaway: The modern novel begins, by many accounts, with Cervantes.

moments.title: Don Quijote part 2
moments.body: Cervantes publishes the second part in response to an unauthorised sequel by 'Avellaneda'.
moments.takeaway: Literary feuds shaped publishing strategy.

now.title: Cervantes now
now.body: The Cervantes Institute (founded 1991) is Spain's global language and cultural body. Don Quijote remains one of the most-translated books.
now.open_questions: How does Don Quijote read 400 years on?

items.reflection: Cervantes invented the figure of the protagonist who has read too much.

moments.title: Fuenteovejuna
moments.body: Lope's play depicts a Castilian village collectively assassinating their tyrannical lord.
moments.takeaway: Spanish Golden Age theatre engaged politics through villages, not princes.

moments.title: La vida es sueno
moments.body: Calderon's play asks whether life is dream or reality.
moments.takeaway: Spanish Baroque drama wrestled with philosophical questions.

moments.title: Lope dies
moments.body: Lope's catalogue includes hundreds of plays. The genre comedia nueva blends comic and tragic, high and low.
moments.takeaway: Some writers produced industrial volumes of work.

now.title: Golden Age theatre now
now.body: Almagro's annual festival keeps Golden Age repertory alive. School syllabuses include both Lope and Calderon.
now.open_questions: How do we stage 17th-century plays for 21st-century audiences?

items.reflection: Spain's Golden Age made theatre a national habit.

moments.title: Velazquez at court
moments.body: Velazquez becomes court painter to Philip IV at 24.
moments.takeaway: Spanish art's golden age was court art.

moments.title: Las Meninas
moments.body: Velazquez paints himself painting, the Infanta Margarita, courtiers and the reflected royal couple.
moments.takeaway: A court group portrait became a meditation on representation.

moments.title: Velazquez dies
moments.body: Velazquez dies after designing decorations for the marriage of Maria Theresa to Louis XIV.
moments.takeaway: Court painters served diplomacy as much as art.

now.title: Velazquez now
now.body: Las Meninas remains the Prado's central painting. Picasso's 58 variations (1957) put it back in dialogue with modern art.
now.open_questions: What other Spanish Golden Age painters deserve global attention?

items.reflection: A single painting keeps four centuries of viewers in conversation.

moments.title: Spanish Armada defeated
moments.body: Storms and English fireships defeat the Armada, beginning a slow Spanish naval decline.
moments.takeaway: Weather decided geopolitics.

moments.title: Peace of Westphalia
moments.body: Spain recognises Dutch independence after 80 years of war.
moments.takeaway: Long wars usually end exhausted.

moments.title: Spanish-American War
moments.body: Spain loses Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines in months. 'El Desastre' triggers a national soul-searching.
moments.takeaway: Empires can collapse in a single year.

now.title: Imperial memory
now.body: The Generation of '98 (Unamuno, Machado, Baroja) responded to the 1898 trauma in literature.
now.open_questions: How does Spain remember 400 years of empire?

items.reflection: Spain spent three centuries losing what it gained in fifty years.

moments.title: Peninsular War
moments.body: Napoleon's invasion provokes the first 'guerrilla' (Spanish for 'little war') and ends with French withdrawal.
moments.takeaway: Modern asymmetric warfare gets its name from Spain.

moments.title: Third of May 1808
moments.body: Goya paints the execution of Madrid civilians by French troops.
moments.takeaway: Modern history painting began with depicting victims.

moments.title: Cadiz Constitution
moments.body: The first liberal constitution of Spain is drafted under siege.
moments.takeaway: Modern constitutions could be drafted in besieged cities.

now.title: 19th-century memory
now.body: Goya's Disasters of War remain a benchmark for war art. The 1812 constitution is celebrated in liberal anniversaries.
now.open_questions: What does the Peninsular War mean to contemporary Spanish politics?

items.reflection: Spain's 19th century was a series of fractures.

moments.title: Mexican independence struggle begins
moments.body: Hidalgo's 'Grito de Dolores' on 16 September 1810 ignites Mexican independence.
moments.takeaway: Latin American independence was triggered by Spain's Napoleonic crisis.

moments.title: Bolivar at Boyaca
moments.body: Bolivar's victory at Boyaca cements his role as Latin American liberator.
moments.takeaway: Single battles can found nations.

moments.title: Bolivar dies
moments.body: Bolivar's dream of a unified Gran Colombia collapses; he dies disillusioned.
moments.takeaway: Liberators do not always like what comes next.

now.title: Bolivar's legacy
now.body: Bolivar's image remains central in Venezuela and Colombia. The Bolivarian Revolution rebranded politics in 21st-century Venezuela.
now.open_questions: What unites Latin America now?

items.reflection: Most of today's Latin American nations were Spanish colonies until the 1820s.

moments.title: Civil War begins
moments.body: Generals' coup against the Republic begins three years of civil war. International Brigades fight on the Republican side.
moments.takeaway: Spain's war was a rehearsal for World War II.

moments.title: Guernica bombed
moments.body: German aircraft destroy the town of Guernica. Picasso paints his canvas in response.
moments.takeaway: Air bombing of civilians entered modern war here.

moments.title: Franco wins
moments.body: Republicans surrender. Franco rules until his death in 1975.
moments.takeaway: Spain spent four decades under dictatorship.

now.title: Civil War memory
now.body: Spain's 2022 Democratic Memory Law funds exhumations of unmarked graves. Franco's body was moved from the Valley of the Fallen in 2019.
now.open_questions: How does Spain reconcile with civil war and dictatorship memory?

items.reflection: Spain's 20th century is impossible to understand without the Civil War.

moments.title: Franco dies
moments.body: Franco dies in November 1975. Juan Carlos I becomes king.
moments.takeaway: Dictatorships sometimes end with their leader's death.

moments.title: Constitution approved
moments.body: Spain's first democratic constitution since the 1930s establishes a parliamentary monarchy with autonomous communities.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional design encoded both democracy and regional diversity.

moments.title: 23-F coup attempt
moments.body: Civil guards seize the Cortes. Juan Carlos's televised address against the coup is credited with saving democracy.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional monarchy survived its closest test.

now.title: Democracy today
now.body: Juan Carlos abdicated in 2014 amid scandal; Felipe VI succeeded. Spain's parliamentary democracy faces pressure from both regionalism and economic crisis.
now.open_questions: What is the future of Spain's 1978 settlement?

items.reflection: Spain's democracy is younger than many other European countries'.

moments.title: Catalan statute
moments.body: Catalonia regains autonomy and recognises Catalan as a co-official language.
moments.takeaway: Spain's regional system was a post-Franco settlement.

moments.title: New statute
moments.body: A revised statute is partly struck down by Spain's Constitutional Court in 2010, fuelling independence sentiment.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional review can radicalise politics.

moments.title: Independence referendum
moments.body: An illegal referendum is held; Catalan leaders are tried for sedition. Police violence at polling stations draws international attention.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional crisis remains live.

now.title: Catalonia today
now.body: Pardons (2021) and amnesty law (2024) shape ongoing tension. Catalan language policy remains contested.
now.open_questions: Where does Spanish federalism settle?

items.reflection: Spain has always been many countries inside one.

moments.title: Romancero gitano
moments.body: Lorca's Gypsy Ballads bring Andalusian themes into modernist verse.
moments.takeaway: Spanish modernism was deeply regional.

moments.title: La Barraca
moments.body: Lorca tours rural Spain with a student theatre troupe, performing classical theatre.
moments.takeaway: Modernist artists could be cultural workers.

moments.title: Lorca executed
moments.body: Lorca is shot by Nationalist forces. His body has never been definitively located.
moments.takeaway: Civil war killed Spain's leading poet at 38.

now.title: Lorca today
now.body: Lorca's work is global, translated and performed worldwide. Searches for his remains continue.
now.open_questions: What does it mean that his grave remains unfound?

items.reflection: Spain's most translated poet died at his country's hands.

moments.title: Borges's Ficciones
moments.body: Borges's stories shape global short fiction. He never wins the Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Influence and prizes do not always align.

moments.title: Cien anos de soledad
moments.body: Garcia Marquez's novel of Macondo defines magical realism for a generation.
moments.takeaway: A single novel can define a region's literary brand.

moments.title: Vargas Llosa wins Nobel
moments.body: Vargas Llosa's Nobel completes the Boom's institutional recognition.
moments.takeaway: Major literary movements can sustain decades.

now.title: Latin American literature today
now.body: Roberto Bolano (2666, 2004), Isabel Allende and Valeria Luiselli continue the tradition. Spanish-language fiction sells globally.
now.open_questions: What follows the Boom?

items.reflection: Spanish-language literature includes more Latin Americans than Spaniards.

moments.title: Un chien andalou
moments.body: The surrealist short film opens with the eye-slicing scene that still shocks.
moments.takeaway: Spanish cinema began in surrealism.

moments.title: La Movida and Almodovar
moments.body: Post-Franco Madrid's countercultural movement frames Almodovar's early films.
moments.takeaway: Dictatorship's end produced cultural release.

moments.title: Cuaron's Roma wins Oscars
moments.body: Cuaron's Mexican film wins Best Director and Best Foreign Language Film.
moments.takeaway: Spanish-language cinema reached global recognition.

now.title: Hispanic cinema today
now.body: Mexican directors (Cuaron, Inarritu, Del Toro) sweep major awards. Spanish series (La Casa de Papel) dominate Netflix.
now.open_questions: What is Spanish-language cinema's next wave?

items.reflection: Hispanic cinema crosses borders that Hispanic politics doesn't.

moments.title: Demoiselles d'Avignon
moments.body: Picasso's painting opens Cubism. He spends most of his life in France but identifies as Spanish.
moments.takeaway: Spanish modernism is partly Parisian by address.

moments.title: The Persistence of Memory
moments.body: Dali's melting clocks become the global emblem of Surrealism.
moments.takeaway: Spanish painters defined 20th-century art.

moments.title: Guernica
moments.body: Picasso paints Guernica for the Spanish Pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exposition.
moments.takeaway: Spanish artists could refuse to live in Franco's Spain.

now.title: Spanish modernism now
now.body: Guernica returned to Spain in 1981 after Franco's death, now at the Reina Sofia.
now.open_questions: Which works should be returned and when?

items.reflection: Three Spanish artists shaped what 20th-century painting looked like.

moments.title: Sagrada Familia begun
moments.body: Gaudi takes over the basilica's design a year after construction begins. He works on it for 43 years.
moments.takeaway: Architectural projects can outlast their architects.

moments.title: Gaudi dies
moments.body: Gaudi is hit by a tram while walking to confession; he is at first mistaken for a beggar.
moments.takeaway: Spain's leading architect died unrecognised.

moments.title: Sagrada Familia projected completion
moments.body: The basilica is projected to be completed on the centenary of Gaudi's death (delayed by pandemic).
moments.takeaway: Some projects span generations.

now.title: Gaudi today
now.body: Seven Gaudi sites in Barcelona are UNESCO World Heritage. Tourism funds the Sagrada Familia's construction.
now.open_questions: What buildings of our era will take 150 years to build?

items.reflection: Spain's most visited landmark is still under construction.

moments.title: First flamenco cafes
moments.body: 'Cafes cantantes' bring flamenco from private events into public performance.
moments.takeaway: Folk traditions become public art forms through specific venues.

moments.title: Concurso de Cante Jondo
moments.who: Manuel de Falla and Federico Garcia Lorca, Granada
moments.body: Falla and Lorca organise a flamenco festival to preserve the tradition's depth.
moments.takeaway: Cultural figures rescue traditions from commodification.

moments.title: Flamenco named UNESCO heritage
moments.body: Flamenco is inscribed on the list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
moments.takeaway: International recognition shapes preservation politics.

now.title: Flamenco today
now.body: Rosalia's fusion of flamenco with pop reaches global audiences. Traditional festivals continue in Andalusia.
now.open_questions: Where does fusion end and tradition begin?

items.reflection: Flamenco belongs to Roma communities, Andalusia and the world simultaneously.

moments.title: Mi noche triste
moments.body: Gardel records the first 'tango cancion', shaping the genre's vocal tradition.
moments.takeaway: Single recordings can establish genres.

moments.title: Salsa emerges
moments.who: New York Puerto Rican and Cuban musicians
moments.body: Salsa develops from Cuban son and other styles in New York's Spanish Harlem.
moments.takeaway: Latin music's diaspora identity is part of its origin.

moments.title: Despacito breaks records
moments.body: The song becomes the first Spanish-language YouTube video to top 6 billion views.
moments.takeaway: Spanish-language music reaches global mainstream.

now.title: Latin music today
now.body: Reggaeton, Latin trap and bachata dominate Spotify global charts. Bad Bunny tops the world's most streamed lists.
now.open_questions: What is the next Latin music wave?

items.reflection: Spanish-language music is now mainstream global pop.

moments.title: Revolution begins
moments.body: Madero's call to arms ends Porfirio Diaz's 31-year dictatorship.
moments.takeaway: Single appeals can launch revolutions.

moments.title: Mexican Constitution
moments.body: The 1917 constitution includes land reform, labour rights and anti-clericalism.
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary constitutions were socially radical.

moments.title: PRI founded
moments.body: What becomes the PRI rules Mexico for 71 years.
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary parties can institutionalise.

now.title: Mexico today
now.body: Sheinbaum's election (2024) makes her Mexico's first woman president. The Mexican drug war shapes politics.
now.open_questions: What does the Mexican Revolution still mean to Mexicans?

items.reflection: Mexico's 20th century was shaped by a decade of civil war.

moments.title: Castro enters Havana
moments.who: Fidel Castro and 26th of July Movement
moments.body: Castro's guerrillas overthrow Batista on 1 January 1959.
moments.takeaway: Cold War politics ran through Caribbean islands.

moments.title: Missile Crisis
moments.body: Soviet missiles in Cuba bring nuclear war within days.
moments.takeaway: Small islands held global futures.

moments.title: US-Cuba thaw
moments.body: Diplomatic relations restored; partly reversed under Trump.
moments.takeaway: Cold War legacies persist.

now.title: Cuba today
now.body: Cuba faces economic crisis and emigration. Raul and Fidel are dead; Diaz-Canel leads.
now.open_questions: What is Cuba's path now?

items.reflection: Cuba's revolution shaped half a century of Latin American politics.

moments.title: Allende elected
moments.body: Allende becomes the first elected Marxist president of a Latin American country.
moments.takeaway: Democratic socialism had its Latin American moment.

moments.title: Pinochet coup
moments.body: On 11 September 1973, Pinochet's coup overthrows Allende. Allende dies in the presidential palace.
moments.takeaway: Cold War politics killed Latin American democracy.

moments.title: Pinochet arrested in London
moments.body: Pinochet's arrest under universal jurisdiction sets a precedent for international human rights law.
moments.takeaway: Dictators can face justice abroad.

now.title: Chile today
now.body: Chile rejected a new constitution in 2022 referenda. The shadow of Pinochet remains in Chilean politics.
now.open_questions: How does Chile reconcile with the Pinochet years?

items.reflection: Chile's modern democracy was rebuilt on top of mass atrocity.

moments.title: Modern bullfighting begins
moments.body: Romero introduces the use of the muleta and the killing sword.
moments.takeaway: What looks 'traditional' often has a specific date of invention.

moments.title: Catalan ban
moments.body: Catalonia bans bullfighting, partly as political distinction from Madrid.
moments.takeaway: Regional politics shape cultural regulation.

moments.title: Spanish Constitutional Court
moments.body: The Court rules bullfighting is national heritage and overturns Catalonia's ban.
moments.takeaway: National heritage status protects controversial practices.

now.title: Bullfighting today
now.body: Audiences are declining and public subsidy is debated. Some autonomous communities limit or ban it.
now.open_questions: Will bullfighting survive another generation?

items.reflection: Tradition is contested wherever it persists.

moments.title: San Fermin moved to July
moments.body: The feast of San Fermin is moved to July; the bull run develops over centuries.
moments.takeaway: Festivals are made by accretion.

moments.title: Hemingway in Pamplona
moments.body: Hemingway publishes The Sun Also Rises, making San Fermin globally famous.
moments.takeaway: Tourism can be triggered by a single novel.

moments.title: First Tomatina
moments.body: A scuffle at a parade in Bunol begins what becomes an annual tomato-throwing festival.
moments.takeaway: Some traditions begin in fights.

now.title: Festivals today
now.body: Mass tourism strains local communities. Animal welfare concerns target the bull run.
now.open_questions: Can festival traditions survive their tourist success?

items.reflection: Spain's festivals make ordinary calendars extraordinary.

moments.title: Paella in Valencia
moments.body: Paella emerges as a one-pan rice dish for fieldworkers, with rabbit, snails and beans before saffron and seafood.
moments.takeaway: National dishes are often rural and regional.

moments.title: First tapas bar concept popularised
moments.body: Hemingway helps popularise tapas internationally, though small dishes were eaten with drinks for centuries.
moments.takeaway: Eating styles travel through expat writers.

moments.title: Mediterranean Diet inscribed
moments.body: The Mediterranean diet, including Spanish cuisine, is named intangible heritage.
moments.takeaway: Eating became inscribed as heritage.

now.title: Spanish food today
now.body: Iberico ham, olive oil and rioja anchor major export industries. Chefs like Ferran Adria reshaped global cuisine.
now.open_questions: What will define Spanish food in the next generation?

items.reflection: Spanish cuisine became a global brand built on regional traditions.

moments.title: Nebrija's grammar
moments.body: The first grammar of any modern European vernacular is published as 'companion to empire'.
moments.takeaway: Language and empire moved together.

moments.title: Real Academia Espanola founded
moments.body: RAE is founded on the model of the Academie francaise. Its motto: 'Limpia, fija y da esplendor' (Cleans, fixes and gives splendour).
moments.takeaway: Language academies were 18th-century institutions.

moments.title: Association of Spanish language academies
moments.body: RAE and 22 academies across Latin America and the Philippines coordinate norms.
moments.takeaway: Spanish is governed by networked academies, not a single one.

now.title: Spanish today
now.body: Around 500 million native speakers make Spanish the second most-spoken native language (after Mandarin). The US has more Spanish speakers than Spain.
now.open_questions: Whose Spanish becomes the global standard?

items.reflection: Spanish belongs to more countries than any other Western European language.
